venue: Crypto.com Arena, Los Angeles, CA, United States

items.fight_news: Joshua Van brings the flyweight belt into the UFC 331 main event with a 17-2 record after winning the title from Alexandre Pantoja at UFC 323. The rematch gives users a cleaner championship read than their first meeting, which ended after Pantoja suffered an early arm and elbow injury.

Pantoja is listed at 30-6 and returns as the No. 1 contender after a four-defense title reign. His resume still carries elite flyweight weight: wins over Brandon Royval, Steve Erceg, Kai Asakura, and Kai Kara-France kept him at the top before the injury loss to Van.

The public stakes are unusually simple for a rematch: Van can validate his championship run with a full-fight win over the former titleholder, while Pantoja can frame the first result as unfinished business if he reclaims the belt in Los Angeles.

Van is only 24, and UFC Brazil credited him with the highest significant-strike pace in flyweight history at 8.43 landed per minute. That makes this a youth-and-output championship defense against one of the division's most accomplished veterans.

Arman Tsarukyan enters the five-round co-main event as a No. 2 lightweight contender with a 23-3 record. UFC's announcement highlights a five-fight winning streak that includes a submission of Dan Hooker and a decision over Charles Oliveira.

Mauricio Ruffy is listed as the No. 7 lightweight at 14-2, and the booking gives him a fast route into title-range relevance. His recent profile is built around stoppage momentum, including a June knockout of Michael Chandler at UFC Freedom 250.

This fight is one of the clearest contender filters on the card. Tsarukyan is defending his near-title position, while Ruffy can collapse the usual lightweight ladder if his striking translates against a proven elite grappler.

MMA Fighting reported Tsarukyan calling the bout a do-or-die moment for his title chances. That adds real context to a non-title co-main event because a win likely keeps him in the championship conversation, while a loss would reset a long climb.

Patricio Pitbull is listed at 37-9 and gets a ranked featherweight slot against Dooho Choi. His long championship-level career makes this a veteran name fight, not a normal mid-card featherweight booking.

Dooho Choi enters at 17-4-1 and is the betting favorite on UFC's event listing. For casual users, the fight reads as a familiar action striker meeting a decorated veteran whose experience spans many more high-stakes rounds.

The No. 15 featherweight tag attached to the bout gives it standings value even with both men carrying established names. A win helps either fighter stay attached to the ranked conversation in a crowded division.

Renato Moicano is listed at 21-7-1 and returns to lightweight for a rematch with Brian Ortega. The UFC card marks Moicano as the ranked lightweight name, giving him a chance to turn a familiar opponent into fresh divisional progress.

Brian Ortega is listed at 16-5 and brings elite featherweight history into a lightweight matchup. The bout is easy to frame for public users: two known submission threats meeting again, now with weight-class context changing the read.

Because both fighters are recognizable grappling-first names, the matchup carries more fan interest than a standard lightweight main-card fight. Moicano has the current divisional ranking, while Ortega has the former title-contender aura.

Alonzo Menifield is listed as the No. 14 light heavyweight with an 18-6-1 record. His presence gives this main-card opener a known UFC power profile against an unbeaten opponent trying to break into the rankings picture.

Iwo Baraniewski comes in at 9-0 and gets a major platform in Los Angeles. An undefeated record against a ranked veteran creates a straightforward prospect test: either the newcomer announces himself, or Menifield protects the established tier.

The public style hook is ranked knockout threat versus unbeaten upside. Menifield has the UFC experience and physical danger, while Baraniewski's perfect record keeps users from treating the bout like a one-way veteran showcase.
Gable Steveson is listed at 4-0 and receives a prominent heavyweight prelim slot. His Olympic wrestling background keeps attention high even though his professional MMA record is still developing.

Sean Sharaf is listed at 4-2 and has pushed back publicly on the promotion around Steveson. That gives the fight a clear narrative beyond records: Sharaf is trying to turn a spotlight built around his opponent into his own UFC statement.

The public matchup reads as decorated wrestling pedigree against a heavyweight looking to expose inexperience. Steveson's athletic upside is obvious, but four professional MMA fights leave meaningful unknowns in striking defense and extended exchanges.

Marlon Vera brings a 23-12-1 record and a ranked bantamweight label into a prelim matchup with Charles Jourdain. Vera's name value makes this one of the most recognizable non-main-card fights at UFC 331.
Charles Jourdain is listed at 18-8-1 and continues his run in a lower-weight matchup after being known for featherweight action fights. Beating Vera would give him a clear ranked bantamweight result.

The broad fan read is pressure, toughness, and late-fight danger against movement, activity, and combination work. Vera has the bigger bantamweight resume, while Jourdain has the chance to use pace to change how users view him in the division.

Tai Tuivasa is listed at 14-10 and remains one of the card's most familiar heavyweights. His recent record has been rough, but his power and name recognition keep the matchup immediately relevant for users.

Robelis Despaigne is listed at 6-2 and brings a striking-based heavyweight profile against Tuivasa. The booking has a simple public hook: two dangerous heavyweights with little room for defensive mistakes.
This is the highest-volatility fight on the prelims. Tuivasa has longer UFC experience, while Despaigne's size, athleticism, and finishing threat make the bout feel live from the opening exchange.

Edmen Shahbazyan is listed at 16-6 and draws Brunno Ferreira in a middleweight prelim. Shahbazyan's UFC story remains familiar: early promise, difficult setbacks, and continued chances to stabilize against dangerous opposition.

Brunno Ferreira enters at 15-4 and adds another Brazilian presence to the Los Angeles card. His finishing reputation makes this a meaningful test for Shahbazyan's ability to manage threat without losing offensive confidence.

The public style setup is clean boxing and early speed against physical power and finishing danger. Neither fighter is hard to explain to users: Shahbazyan needs control, Ferreira needs moments that change the temperature fast.

Giga Chikadze is listed at 15-6 and remains a known featherweight striker. His kickboxing background keeps the matchup readable for public users, especially against an opponent comfortable making fights physical.
Joanderson Brito enters at 19-5-1 and gives the early prelims another strong Brazilian name. His record and pressure profile make him more than a showcase opponent for Chikadze's striking.

This fight has a clear style contrast: Chikadze wants distance, kicking lanes, and clean resets, while Brito wants contact, collisions, and exchanges that make the technical striker work at a less comfortable pace.
Casey O'Neill is listed at 11-2 and ranked No. 12 at women's flyweight on the UFC 331 card. The bout gives her a chance to defend her spot against a nearby ranked Brazilian challenger.
Eduarda Moura is listed at 12-2 and ranked No. 13, making this one of the card's cleanest standings fights. A win would likely let Moura move directly into O'Neill's lane in the flyweight rankings.

The public stakes are rankings and divisional sorting rather than star power. Both women are close enough on the ladder that a clear winner can leave Los Angeles with a much stronger case for a bigger name next.
Ryan Gandra is listed at 10-1 and appears on the UFC 331 prelims against Ozzy Diaz. His record gives the matchup a prospect feel even without a ranking attached.

Ozzy Diaz is listed at 10-4 and brings more losses but also more visible adversity into the matchup. For public users, this is a test of whether Gandra's cleaner record holds up against a tougher, more experienced opponent.

The fight sits deeper on the card, but it still has prediction value because both men carry finishing upside. Gandra has the cleaner profile, while Diaz has the kind of power that can disrupt a prospect narrative quickly.

bouts.title: Michael Aswell Jr. vs. Joosang Yoo

items.fight_news: Michael Aswell Jr. is listed at 11-5 and opens the UFC 331 lineup against Joosang Yoo. His record shows more professional mileage, which can matter in a first-fight-of-the-night spot where composure is often tested early.
Joosang Yoo is listed at 9-1 and gives the featherweight opener a clean prospect angle. A win would help him turn a quiet early prelim placement into a useful resume step.

The public read is experience against sharper record optics. Aswell has seen more outcomes across his career, while Yoo has less damage on the record and a chance to make the opener feel like an arrival.
